item.title: Inside the Telecom Attack Surface: SS7, BGP Hijacking, and the Technical Reality of Nation-State Intrusions
item.description: Source: Cyble / Source attributes: Singapore / Vendor / Primary / Categories: Security, Threat Intel, Vulnerability, Exploit, Zero-Day, Patch, APT, Mobile, Endpoint, Network, Detection, Threat Actor / Topics: Salt Typhoon, Apple/iOS, Cisco, Ivanti, Network Edge, Vulnerability, Exploit, Zero-Day, APT / Priority: Critical (100) / SOC: 100 / Confidence: High (100) / Focus: APT / targeted campaign (rank 6) / Reference count: 1 / Reasons: focus: APT / targeted campaign, EN attack activity, EN active exploit/PoC/zero-day, EN detection/analysis, EN targeted/APT/state-backed, EN critical sector, APT/campaign priority, coherent attack event, target and impact context, detection evidence context, critical sector, primary references 1 / Summary: Nation-state operators rarely need a zero-day to get inside a carrier. Much of the telecom stack still runs protocols designed when every participant was a known, trusted operator. SS7 assumes that the node sending a request has a legitimate reason to send it. BGP assumes a network announcing a route actually owns it. Attackers who understand those assumptions can operate inside a carrier for years without triggering a single alert. For telecom CISOs and SOC teams, defending this environment starts with understanding how these attacks actually work.
